His replacement, African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe, will be sworn in as South Africa's president Thursday. The resignations, which include Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, will take effect Thursday when Mbeki steps down, a government statement said. "All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement said. The finance minister's assistant told CNN that Manuel is willing to serve in the new government, if needed. Three deputy ministers have also tendered their resignations, a government statement said. A spokesman for South Africa's ruling party, the African National Congress, confirmed that it has named Motlanthe as its choice to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe will stay in office until elections in the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win. Earlier this month, the ANC asked Mbeki to step down after a judge threw out the corruption, fraud and racketeering case against Zuma -- Mbeki's political arch rival. The judge called the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference. Mbeki -- who has been South Africa's president for nearly 10 years -- spoke of some of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation on Sunday during a televised address.  Watch the significance of Mbeki "falling on the sword" » . "I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said. Mbeki said the country still has economic, corruption and crime challenges to face in the future. And he gave his vote of confidence to the country's next leader without naming who that leader would be. Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced Saturday that the party -- which Mbeki has been involved with since his teens -- had asked him to leave before his term was up. Mbeki agreed to do so, he said. The case against Zuma -- who replaced Mbeki as ANC president last year -- was thrown out in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority recharged him. Judge Chris Nicholson made no ruling on Zuma's guilt or innocence, and he could be recharged. Political observers doubted that would happen because of Zuma's popularity, particularly with the Communist Party and trade unions. Zuma has denied the charges. He said the case was politically motivated, and harmed his chances to become the ANC's presidential nominee. He could have faced at least 15 years in jail if convicted of accepting bribes from a company that got a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal. He also faced charges of having a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes for Zuma and using Zuma's political influence to benefit his businesses. Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics alleged he pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma. Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing deal between Zimbabwe's political rivals, who signed the agreement on Monday in an effort to put aside the violent past and end the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March. Under it, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, has become prime minister and the coordinator of government affairs.

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)** — Ten South African cabinet ministers and the deputy president have tendered their resignations as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to step down. The wave of departures follows Mbeki’s televised national address on Sunday, in which he formally announced his resignation. 

African National Congress (ANC) Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe has been designated to succeed Mbeki and will be sworn in as President on Thursday.

According to government sources, Mbeki’s initial announcement prompted several cabinet members to threaten a walkout, though the outgoing president personally urged them to remain in office. An official statement confirmed that the resignations—which include Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, alongside three deputy ministers—will take effect Thursday in tandem with Mbeki's departure.

"All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement read. An aide to Trevor Manuel informed CNN that the finance minister remains open to serving in the new administration if requested.

Motlanthe will hold office until national elections in the spring of next year—a contest widely expected to be won by ANC President Jacob Zuma.

The political upheaval follows the ANC’s formal request for Mbeki to step down prior to the end of his term. The decision came after High Court Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed a high-profile corruption, fraud, and racketeering case against Zuma, Mbeki’s chief political rival. The judge declared the proceedings invalid and cited political interference by Mbeki’s administration.

ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe stated on Saturday that the party—with which Mbeki, 66, has been affiliated since his teenage years—asked him to relinquish the presidency to ensure "stability within the country" and maintain a "stable and unified" movement. Mbeki acquiesced to the party's request.

The legal battle surrounding Zuma has been fraught. Although an earlier case was thrown out in September 2006 before being reinstated by the National Prosecuting Authority, Judge Nicholson’s recent ruling made no determination on Zuma's guilt or innocence, technically leaving open the possibility of recharged proceedings. However, political analysts consider a renewed prosecution unlikely given Zuma’s immense popularity, particularly among trade unions and the South African Communist Party.

Zuma, who ousted Mbeki as ANC leader last year, has consistently denied all charges, maintaining they were politically motivated attempts to derail his presidential candidacy. Had he been convicted of accepting bribes from a firm involved in a multibillion-dollar arms deal, or of maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik—who is currently serving a 15-year sentence—Zuma would have faced a minimum of 15 years in prison.

Reflecting on his decade-long presidency after succeeding Nelson Mandela in June 1999, Mbeki used his Sunday address to highlight his administration's legacy, even as critics accused him of orchestrating the charges against Zuma.

"I depart this office knowing that many men and women in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said, symbolic of a leader "falling on his sword."

Mbeki noted that under his stewardship, South Africa experienced its longest period of sustained economic growth in history and engaged in unprecedented social outreach for the impoverished. While acknowledging that the nation continues to face significant challenges regarding crime, corruption, and the economy, Mbeki offered a vote of confidence in the country's next leader, though he stopped short of naming him.

Despite his domestic troubles, Mbeki leaves office following a major diplomatic success. Just days prior, he brokered a landmark power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe’s political rivals, signed on Monday. The deal seeks to end months of violence and political paralysis following disputed national elections in March, establishing long-serving leader Robert Mugabe as President while appointing his political rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, as Prime Minister and coordinator of government affairs.

The catalyst for the party's demand was a recent court ruling involving Jacob Zuma, Mbeki’s key political adversary who replaced him as ANC leader last year. Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed a case brought by the National Prosecuting Authority that charged Zuma with fraud, corruption, and racketeering. The judge deemed the proceedings invalid and pointed to political interference by Mbeki’s government, though he made no determination regarding Zuma's actual guilt or innocence. 

Zuma had previously faced potential sentences of 15 years or more over allegations of accepting bribes from a company involved in a massive military procurement deal, as well as maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial advisor, Schabir Shaik—who is currently serving a 15-year prison term for soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf. **Title:** The Fall of Mbeki: How a Power Struggle Reshaped South African Politics

In September 2008, South Africa experienced its most profound political convulsion since the end of apartheid. Facing intense political turmoil sparked by allegations of executive interference in the judiciary, President Thabo Mbeki formally tendered his resignation. The historic decision came after the National Executive Committee (NEC) of the ruling African National Congress (ANC) officially "recalled" him from office, marking a dramatic end to a presidency defined by economic growth, diplomatic ambition, and deep-seated party rivalries.

### The Catalyst: Judicial Controversy and Internal Division

The roots of Mbeki’s downfall lay in a bitter, years-long power struggle between himself and his former deputy, Jacob Zuma. Mbeki had dismissed Zuma as deputy president in 2005 after Zuma was implicated in a high-profile corruption scandal. However, Zuma retained immense popularity among the party’s grassroots, trade unions, and left-wing factions. In late 2007, Zuma defeated Mbeki for the ANC presidency at the party's conference in Polokwane, effectively creating a dual power structure in South Africa: Zuma led the ruling party, while Mbeki led the state.

The breaking point arrived in September 2008, when High Court Judge Piet Nicholson dismissed corruption charges against Zuma on a technicality. Crucially, the judge’s ruling suggested that Mbeki’s administration—specifically the Ministry of Justice and public prosecutors—had engaged in political interference to manipulate the timing of the charges against Zuma. 

Although Mbeki vehemently denied the allegations, the ruling gave Zuma’s allies within the ANC the political ammunition they needed. After a marathon 14-hour meeting, the ANC’s executive committee announced it was recalling Mbeki, effectively forcing him to step down months before his term was set to expire.

### A Formal Exit and the Domino Effect

On the evening of Sunday, September 21, 2008, Mbeki addressed the nation in a solemn, televised broadcast. Demonstrating deference to the constitutional framework and party discipline, he announced his intention to resign as President of the Republic once Parliament accepted the decision.

"I have been a loyal member of the African National Congress for 50 years," Mbeki stated, maintaining his dignity while firmly rejecting the allegations that had brought down his presidency. "I remain convinced that the allegations that the cabinet or I interfered with the National Prosecuting Authority are unfounded."

Mbeki’s departure immediately triggered a secondary crisis within the executive branch. In a show of solidarity—or out of reluctance to serve under a new faction—a wave of high-level resignations destabilized the government. Ten cabinet ministers and Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka submitted their resignations. 

The mass exit included key figures such as Minister of Finance Trevor Manuel, a move that sent shockwaves through international markets and caused the South African rand to plummet. Although Manuel was quickly persuaded to remain in government to maintain economic stability, the exodus laid bare the deep fractures within the ruling party.

### The Interim Stewardship of Kgalema Motlanthe

To navigate the nation through the political crisis and restore public confidence, Parliament elected Kgalema Motlanthe as interim president. Motlanthe, then the deputy president of the ANC, was widely regarded as a calm, technocratic, and unifying figure within the party who held the respect of both the Mbeki and Zuma camps.

Sworn in shortly after Mbeki’s departure, Motlanthe made it clear that his primary mandate was continuity. His task was not to forge a new political path, but to steady the ship of state, reassure foreign investors, and oversee a peaceful, orderly transition leading up to the national elections scheduled for the spring of 2009.

### A New Era Begins

The forced resignation of Thabo Mbeki reshaped the trajectory of post-apartheid South Africa. It demonstrated the supreme power of the ANC over the state executive, while simultaneously fracturing the party—leading disgruntled Mbeki loyalists to break away and form a new opposition party, the Congress of the People (COPE).

More significantly, Mbeki’s exit cleared the final political obstacles for Jacob Zuma. Following the April 2009 general election, in which the ANC secured a decisive victory under Motlanthe's caretaker leadership, Parliament officially elected Jacob Zuma as President of South Africa. The transition marked the definitive close of the Mbeki era and the beginning of a turbulent new chapter in the nation's democratic journey.

**Johannesburg: The Beating Heart of South Africa**

High on the dusty plains of the Witwatersrand plateau lies **Johannesburg**, the largest and most dynamic city in **South Africa**. Known affectionately as Jo’burg, Jozi, or *eGoli*—the Zulu word for the "City of Gold"—this sprawling metropolis is much more than just a transit stop; it is the economic, cultural, and creative engine of Southern **Africa**.

The story of Johannesburg is inextricably linked to the precious metal beneath its soil. Founded almost overnight following the discovery of gold in 1886, the town rapidly transformed from a rough-and-tumble mining camp into a powerful financial hub. Yet, the city’s history is as complex as it is rich. As the heartbeat of the anti-apartheid movement, Johannesburg played a pivotal role in shaping the destiny of modern South Africa. Today, landmark sites like the Apartheid Museum, Constitutional Hill, and the vibrant township of Soweto stand as powerful testaments to the struggle for freedom and human rights. Vilakazi Street in Soweto remains world-famous as the only street in the world once home to two Nobel Peace Prize laureates: Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

In the 21st century, Johannesburg has reinvented itself once again. It has emerged as an unstoppable force of African urban culture, characterized by grit, resilience, and boundless artistic energy. Precincts like Maboneng and Braamfontein have seen a dramatic urban rebirth, transforming once-neglected industrial blocks into trendy neighborhoods filled with street art, indie design studios, contemporary galleries, and bustling rooftop markets. 

The city's sensory landscape is equally compelling. The air vibrates with the sounds of local music, from jazz to the infectious beat of *Amapiano*—a global dance movement born right in Jozi's townships. Its culinary scene offers a melting pot of flavors, blending traditional pan-African dishes with international fine dining.

Despite its reputation as a fast-paced concrete jungle, Johannesburg surprises many with its natural greenery. It is widely recognized as one of the largest man-made urban forests in the world, boasting over ten million trees. Every spring, the cityscape undergoes a dramatic transformation as thousands of Jacaranda trees burst into bloom, painting the suburbs in breathtaking shades of purple.

Johannesburg is a city of contrasts—raw yet sophisticated, deeply historical yet fiercely forward-looking. To truly understand the spirit, struggle, and vibrant future of South Africa, one must look no further than the electrifying energy of Johannesburg.

**South Africa in political shock as President Thabo Mbeki resigns following brutal ANC power struggle**

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)** — South African President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation Sunday in a televised address to the nation, bringing a dramatic and abrupt end to his nine-year presidency following a bruising political feud within the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

Mbeki’s decision comes less than 24 hours after the ANC’s National Executive Committee formally "recalled" him, withdrawing its support for the leader who succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999. 

"I have submitted my letter of resignation to the Speaker of the National Assembly," a somber Mbeki said in his address, maintaining a calm demeanor. "I would like to state that for 14 years, I had the privilege to serve in the executive of our country... I am grateful to the nation and the ANC for giving me the opportunity to serve."

The unprecedented move marks the biggest political upheaval in South Africa since the end of apartheid in 1994, exposing deep fissures within the liberation movement that has governed the country for fourteen years.

### A bitter rivalry reaches its climax

At the heart of Mbeki’s downfall is a fiercely personal and ideological battle with Jacob Zuma, the charismatic populist who ousted Mbeki as ANC party president during a fiery party conference in Polokwane last December.

The breaking point came earlier this month when High Court Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed corruption charges against Zuma on a technicality. Crucially, the judge suggested that Mbeki’s administration had engaged in "political interference" in the National Prosecuting Authority’s decision to charge Zuma.

While Mbeki fiercely denied the allegations on Sunday—calling them "categorically untrue"—Zuma’s allies within the ANC moved swiftly to execute a political coup, demanding Mbeki step down months before his term was scheduled to end in mid-2009.

"We felt that the relationship between the government and the party had been severely damaged," ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe told reporters in Johannesburg, attempting to frame the move as a step toward party unity.

### Cabinet mass exodus triggers economic anxiety

The fallout from Mbeki's resignation was immediate and devastating to government stability. On Tuesday, a wave of high-profile cabinet ministers followed Mbeki out the door, throwing the government into further chaos and sending shockwaves through financial markets.

At least 11 cabinet ministers and several deputy ministers tendered their resignations out of loyalty to Mbeki or a refusal to serve under the current party mandate. Among those resigning was Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka.

The announcement that highly respected Finance Minister Trevor Manuel had also submitted his resignation sent the South African rand tumbling by more than 4% against the U.S. dollar, while stock markets slipped sharply. Manuel later clarified that his resignation was a constitutional formality and that he remained willing to serve the incoming administration, which helped calm jittery foreign investors.

### Motlanthe tapped to steer the ship

To navigate the power vacuum, the ANC has selected party deputy president Kgalema Motlanthe to take over as South Africa’s interim president. 

Motlanthe, a respected former trade union leader and anti-apartheid veteran, is widely viewed as a unifying figure. He is expected to be officially sworn in by parliament later this week and will hold the presidency until general elections are held in early 2009.

Political analysts view Motlanthe as a "safe pair of hands" designed to steady the country and reassure international investors, while clearing the path for Jacob Zuma to run for the presidency next year. Zuma cannot currently assume the state presidency because he does not hold a seat in parliament.

"Motlanthe’s role is to bridge the gap," said Judith February, a political analyst at the Institute for Democracy in South Africa (IDASA). "He has to restore calm, manage a deeply fractured cabinet, and ensure the state apparatus continues to function while the ANC prepares for 2009."

### A complex legacy

Mbeki’s sudden exit leaves behind a complex and disputed legacy.

Internationally, he was lauded as an intellectual strategist who championed an "African Renaissance," playing a pivotal role in creating the New Partnership for Africa's Development (NEPAD) and mediating conflicts in Zimbabwe, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Domestically, his stewardship of the economy ushered in South Africa's longest period of continuous economic growth.

However, his presidency was heavily overshadowed by controversial policies. Mbeki drew fierce international and domestic condemnation for his dissident views on HIV/AIDS, which delayed the rollout of life-saving antiretroviral drugs. Critics also accused his administration of failing to address South Africa's rampant violent crime and lingering economic inequality.

For many South Africans, the sight of a sitting president being ousted by his own party is a stark reminder of the ANC’s absolute dominance over the nation's political landscape.

In his closing remarks, Mbeki urged South Africans to support the incoming administration and safeguard the country’s young democracy.

"We should never play fast and loose with the constitutional order that so many of our people fought to establish," Mbeki said. "I wish the new leadership all the success as they steer our country toward a better life for all."

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the key events of Thabo Mbeki's resignation from the South African presidency in late September 2008.
counterfactuals.output:
The resignation of South African President Thabo Mbeki in late September 2008 was a landmark moment in post-apartheid South African politics. It marked the culmination of a bitter power struggle within the ruling African National Congress (ANC) between Mbeki and his former deputy, Jacob Zuma. 

Here is a summary of the key events:

### 1. The Background and Polokwane Shift
*   **The Mbeki-Zuma Rift:** In 2005, Mbeki dismissed Zuma as the country's Deputy President after Zuma was implicated in a high-profile corruption scandal involving arms deals.
*   **Dec 2007 (Polokwane Conference):** Zuma defeated Mbeki in the ANC internal elections to become the President of the party. This created "two centers of power"—Zuma leading the ruling party, and Mbeki leading the country—setting the stage for Mbeki’s eventual removal.

### 2. The Catalyst: The Nicholson Ruling (September 12, 2008)
*   High Court Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed corruption charges against Jacob Zuma on procedural grounds.
*   Crucially, Judge Nicholson implied in his ruling that Mbeki and his cabinet had engaged in "political meddling" and exerted political pressure on the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) to prosecute Zuma. 
*   Mbeki strongly denied these allegations, but the ruling provided Zuma’s allies within the ANC with the leverage they needed to act.

### 3. The ANC "Recall" (September 20, 2008)
*   Following a tense, 24-hour emergency meeting of the ANC’s National Executive Committee (NEC)—now dominated by Zuma loyalists—ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe announced that the party had decided to **"recall"** Mbeki from his position as President of South Africa.
*   Under the South African Constitution, a party cannot directly dismiss a president, but it can direct its members of parliament to vote the president out. To avoid a constitutional crisis, Mbeki agreed to comply with the party's demand.

### 4. The Resignation Announcement (September 21–22, 2008)
*   **National Address (Sept 21):** Mbeki delivered a televised address to the nation, announcing his resignation. He reiterated that he had never interfered in the judicial process or targeted Zuma.
*   **Formal Letter (Sept 22):** Mbeki officially tendered his resignation letter to Parliament, effective midnight on September 25.

### 5. Cabinet Fallout and Resignations (September 23, 2008)
*   Mbeki’s resignation triggered a wave of high-profile resignations within his government. 
*   Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and 10 cabinet ministers—including respected Finance Minister Trevor Manuel—resigned out of loyalty to Mbeki, sending shockwaves through South Africa’s economic markets (though Manuel was quickly reappointed by the incoming leadership to stabilize the economy).

### 6. The Transition and Legacy (September 25, 2008)
*   **Interim Presidency:** Parliament elected **Kgalema Motlanthe** (then-Deputy President of the ANC) as the interim President to serve until the general elections in April 2009, when Jacob Zuma ultimately assumed the presidency.
*   **Political Splinter:** Dissatisfied Mbeki loyalists left the ANC shortly after to form a new opposition party, the Congress of the People (COPE), marking the first major split in the ANC since it took power in 1994.

**SPECIAL REPORT: SOUTH AFRICA IN UNCHARTERED WATERS AFTER ANC FORCES PRESIDENT MBEKI TO RESIGN**

**JOHANNESBURG** — In the most dramatic political convulsion in South Africa’s post-apartheid history, President Thabo Mbeki has announced his resignation after the ruling African National Congress (ANC) formally withdrew its support for his leadership. 

The decision, handed down by the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC) following an arduous weekend of deliberations, brings a sudden and humiliating end to Mbeki’s nine-year presidency. It has plunged Africa’s largest economy into deep political uncertainty, exposing profound fractures within the liberation movement that has governed South Africa since 1994.

Addressing the nation in a dignified television broadcast, President Mbeki confirmed he had tendered his resignation to the Speaker of Parliament. "I have served our country and people to the best of my ability," Mbeki said, firmly denying allegations that he had abused state power to target his political opponents.

---

### The Catalyst: Judicial Bombshell and Party "Recall"

The catalyst for Mbeki’s downfall was a high-stakes judicial ruling by High Court Judge Chris Nicholson. In dismissing corruption charges against Mbeki’s arch-rival and current ANC President, Jacob Zuma, Judge Nicholson suggested there had been "political interference" at the highest levels of government—implying Mbeki’s administration had orchestrated the legal campaign to destroy Zuma's political career.

Though Mbeki vigorously rejected the judge's findings, the newly ascendant, pro-Zuma wing of the ANC moved swiftly. Exercising a constitutional quirk of South Africa’s parliamentary system—where the majority party effectively appoints the head of state—the ANC "recalled" Mbeki, giving him little choice but to resign before facing a vote of no confidence in Parliament.

---

### A Bittersweet Legacy: The Mbeki Era

Thabo Mbeki, a cerebral, UK-educated diplomat, assumed the presidency in 1999 following the legendary Nelson Mandela. Over his nine years in power, Mbeki accumulated a complex and often polarizing legacy.

**Economic and Global Successes:**
Architect of South Africa's modern macroeconomic framework, Mbeki oversaw the nation’s longest period of sustained economic growth since the 1960s. Under his administration:
* Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth averaged over 4% annually, briefly touching 5%.
* Strict fiscal discipline drastically reduced foreign debt and the state budget deficit.
* Millions of black South Africans entered the middle class, aided by Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) policies.
* Mbeki emerged as a global statesman, championing the "African Renaissance," co-founding the New Partnership for Africa’s Development (NEPAD), and driving the transition from the Organization of African Unity (OAU) to the modern African Union (AU). He played pivotal roles in negotiating peace deals in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Burundi, and Ivory Coast.

**Controversies and Blind Spots:**
Despite these triumphs, Mbeki’s presidency was marred by severe controversies:
* **HIV/AIDS Denialism:** Mbeki’s public skepticism regarding the link between HIV and AIDS, and his delay in rolling out life-saving antiretroviral drugs, drew intense domestic and international condemnation. Health experts estimate this policy led to hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths.
* **Quiet Diplomacy in Zimbabwe:** His reluctance to publicly condemn President Robert Mugabe’s authoritarian turn and economic misrule in neighboring Zimbabwe alienated Western allies and human rights advocates.
* **Technocratic Governance:** Critics often portrayed Mbeki as an aloof, centralized ruler who increasingly insulated himself within the presidency, detaching from the ANC’s working-class base.

---

### The Titanic Rivalry: Mbeki vs. Zuma

At the heart of South Africa’s current political crisis is the decade-long, bitter feud between Mbeki and Jacob Zuma. 

Once close allies within the anti-apartheid struggle, the rift widened in 2005 when Mbeki dismissed Zuma as the nation's Deputy President after Zuma’s financial advisor, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption. Zuma’s supporters viewed the move not as a moral stand against corruption, but as a calculated political execution.

Zuma, a charismatic populist with deep roots in the ANC's labor and youth wings, channeled popular dissatisfaction with Mbeki’s orthodox economic policies. The rivalry culminated in December 2007 at the ANC’s landmark elective conference in Polokwane. In an unprecedented humiliation for a sitting head of state, Zuma defeated Mbeki for the leadership of the ANC, setting off a slow-motion collapse of Mbeki's executive authority.

The Polokwane conference effectively created a dangerous "two centers of power"—with Mbeki controlling the state and Zuma controlling the party. Judge Nicholson's ruling provided the pro-Zuma camp with the final lever needed to remove Mbeki entirely.

---

### Political Fallout: Market Volatility and ANC Splintering

The news of Mbeki’s forced exit sent shockwaves through South Africa’s financial markets. The South African Rand plunged against major currencies, and the Johannesburg Stock Exchange experienced sharp sell-offs amid fears that Mbeki’s pro-business economic policies might be dismantled in favor of left-leaning populist measures advocated by Zuma’s allies in the trade unions (COSATU) and the South African Communist Party (SACP).

Instability deepened when a third of Mbeki's cabinet—including Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka and several key ministers—tendered their resignations out of loyalty to the outgoing president. The financial sector was temporarily panicked when it was reported that highly respected Finance Minister Trevor Manuel had also resigned, though market fears eased after Manuel clarified his willingness to serve under a new administration.

The political reverberations extend far beyond parliament:
* **An Impending ANC Split:** Dissident Mbeki loyalists, led by former Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota and former Gauteng Premier Mbhazima Shilowa, have announced plans to break away from the ANC. This movement is expected to form a new political party—the Congress of the People (COPE)—marking the first major splinter of the ANC since it took power in 1994.
* **Institutional Strain:** The saga has raised alarming questions about the independence of South Africa’s judiciary and prosecutorial agencies, with both camps accusing the other of weaponizing state institutions for political infighting.

---

### The Interim Leadership: Kgalema Motlanthe Takes the Helm

To calm volatile markets and steady the ship of state, the ANC has selected party Deputy President **Kgalema Motlanthe** to serve as South Africa’s interim President until general elections are held in mid-2009.

Motlanthe, a former union leader and political prisoner on Robben Island, is widely regarded as a deeply respected, calm, and unifying figure within the ANC. Uniquely positioned as a bridge between the Mbeki and Zuma camps, Motlanthe’s immediate mandate is to maintain government continuity, reassure foreign investors, and heal the deep wounds within the ruling party.

In his opening statements, Motlanthe moved swiftly to quell economic anxiety, reassuring international markets that the government’s fiscal and monetary policies would remain unchanged.

However, political analysts emphasize that Motlanthe’s presidency is fundamentally a caretaker administration. He is "warming the seat" for Jacob Zuma, who is widely expected to lead the ANC to victory in the upcoming 2009 general elections and formally assume the presidency.

---

### A Watershed Moment for South African Democracy

The recall of Thabo Mbeki marks a definitive turning point in post-apartheid South Africa. While it demonstrates the extraordinary power of the ANC as an institution capable of removing a sitting head of state without military intervention, it simultaneously exposes the vulnerability of the country's governance to internal party feuds.

As South Africa prepares for an uncertain election year, the era of Mandela and Mbeki's technocratic dream has given way to a volatile new political reality—one characterized by a re-energized left, a fragmented ruling party, and a nation wrestling with the balance between rule of law and political power.

### MBEKI RESIGNS: SOUTH AFRICA IN TURMOIL AS ANC FORCES OUT PRESIDENT
**Byline:** Foreign Bureau / Political Desk  
**Dateline:** PRETORIA, South Africa — September 21, 2008  

In an unprecedented political earthquake that has shattered the illusion of post-apartheid stability, Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation as President of South Africa late Sunday evening. 

Bowing to an ultimatum from the ruling African National Congress (ANC), Mbeki’s dramatic downfall marks the end of a solemn, nine-year presidency and signals a decisive triumph for his arch-rival, Jacob Zuma. 

In a televised address to a stunned nation, a somber but composed Mbeki revealed that he had submitted his letter of resignation to the Speaker of the National Assembly. 

"I have tendered my resignation from the position of President of the Republic of South Africa," Mbeki said, speaking from the Union Buildings in Pretoria. "I am convinced that the continued unity of the ANC, the alliance, and the country is paramount."

However, Mbeki used his farewell address to vigorously deny the accusations that led to his political execution. "I would like to state this categorically: that we have never interfered, nor intended to interfere, with the work of the National Prosecuting Authority," he declared.

---

### The Trigger: A Bombshell Court Ruling

The catalyst for Mbeki’s sudden removal came nine days ago in a High Court courtroom in Pietermaritzburg. Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed corruption charges against Jacob Zuma on a technicality, but went much further—accusing Mbeki and his cabinet of "political interference" in the decision to prosecute Zuma.

The ruling provided the ultimate ammunition for Zuma’s allies within the ANC. Following a grueling, 24-hour meeting of the party’s powerful 86-member National Executive Committee (NEC) at a hotel in Benoni, the ANC announced on Saturday that it had decided to "recall" the President.

ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe framed the decision as a necessary move to heal the deeply fractured party. "Our decision is a movement to build unity," Mantashe told reporters, though critics have widely described it as a brutal political purge.

---

### The Roots of the Feud

The bitter power struggle between Mbeki and Zuma has consumed South Africa’s political landscape for years. 

Mbeki dismissed Zuma as the country's Deputy President in 2005 after Zuma was implicated in a landmark arms deal corruption case. Zuma, a charismatic populist with strong backing from the ANC’s Left wing—including trade unions (COSATU) and the Communist Party—spent the next three years mounting a relentless political comeback.

That struggle reached a boiling point in December 2007 at the ANC's national conference in Polokwane, where Zuma ousted Mbeki as ANC party president in a bitter vote. Since then, South Africa has endured a bizarre dual-power dynamic: Mbeki ran the government, while Zuma controlled the ruling party. Yesterday, the party finally crushed the government.

---

### Economic Panic and Cabinet Chaos

The resignation has sent shockwaves through international financial markets, triggering fears of economic instability in Africa’s largest economy. 

The South African Rand plummeted against the US Dollar immediately following the announcement, driven by panic over who will lead the country’s economic policy.

---

### Enter the Caretaker: Motlanthe Steps In

Under the South African Constitution, Parliament must formally elect a new President within 30 days. Because the ANC holds a overwhelming majority in Parliament, the party's choice is guaranteed to take office.

To prevent Jacob Zuma—who does not currently hold a seat in Parliament—from taking power prematurely ahead of the general election expected in April 2009, the ANC has selected party Deputy President **Kgalema Motlanthe** to serve as interim President.

Motlanthe, a respected former trade unionist seen as a calm, unifying figure, will take the helm of a deeply divided nation.

Opposition parties have reacted with a mix of fury and alarm. Democratic Alliance leader Helen Zille condemned the ANC’s decision, accusing Zuma’s faction of undermining the rule of law to protect their leader from criminal prosecution.

"The ANC has put the interests of one man above the interests of the entire country," Zille said. "This is not about principle; this is about revenge."

---

### A Complex Legacy

Mbeki’s exit marks a tragic end for a man once hailed as the intellectual architect of the "African Renaissance."

Taking power from Nelson Mandela in 1999, Mbeki was lauded globally for overseeing South Africa's longest period of uninterrupted economic growth, modernizing infrastructure, and leading peacekeeping missions across the African continent.

* **Quiet Diplomacy in Zimbabwe:** His soft-handed approach to Zimbabwean dictator Robert Mugabe drew fierce international condemnation as Zimbabwe’s economy collapsed.
* **Aloof Governance:** Mbeki was often criticized at home as an aloof, technocratic leader who lost touch with the impoverished masses—a vulnerability Zuma exploited to perfection.

---

### What Lies Ahead?

As night falls on Pretoria, South Africa enters uncharted territory. For the first time since the fall of apartheid in 1994, a democratically elected president has been forced from office not by the voters, but by his own political party.

The political landscape has been permanently altered. Analysts predict that Mbeki's loyalists may break away from the ANC entirely to form a new opposition party, potentially ending the ANC's total dominance of South African politics.

For now, the nation waits anxiously for Kgalema Motlanthe to be sworn in later this week, as Jacob Zuma stands on the precipice of ultimate power, waiting in the wings for 2009.
